questions.prompt: What is the core mistake in the endowment effect?
choices: Letting ownership inflate value beyond what neutral evidence supports
Ignoring every personal use case when pricing an item
Assuming all market prices are perfect

explanation.gentle: Yes. The object feels more valuable mainly because it is already owned.
explanation.direct: Correct. Possession is distorting valuation instead of the price being anchored only in the object's support.
explanation.competitive: That is the trap. Ownership is juicing the number.

questions.prompt: Why can this bias arrive so quickly after ownership begins?
choices: Because keeping the item starts feeling normal while giving it up starts feeling like loss
Because ownership instantly improves the object's quality
Because buyers usually know less than sellers

explanation.gentle: Right. Ownership changes how surrender feels.
explanation.direct: Exactly. The emotional frame shifts fast, so parting with the item can feel costlier than before.
explanation.competitive: That is it. The second it is yours, letting go starts charging a fee.

questions.prompt: Which situation best fits the endowment effect?
choices: A seller asks much more for a used guitar than similar buyers are willing to pay because it feels special to them
A shopper compares several guitars before buying one
A musician replaces an instrument after it breaks

explanation.gentle: Yes. Ownership is making the item feel worth more than the outside market supports.
explanation.direct: Correct. The seller's possession and attachment are inflating the price beyond a neutral valuation.
explanation.competitive: That is the move. The owner glow is marking up the guitar.

questions.prompt: Maya keeps defending an internal tool her team built even though a better external option now exists. What is most likely happening?
choices: Ownership of the tool is inflating its perceived value
The outside tool must secretly be worse in every way
The team is wisely ignoring switching costs

explanation.gentle: Yes. Built-here ownership can make the tool feel more valuable than it currently is.
explanation.direct: The likely distortion is that possession and authorship are carrying the judgment farther than present utility does.
explanation.competitive: That is the bias. The team-built badge is padding the score.

questions.prompt: Evan refuses to cut a weak section from his paper because he wrote it and feels attached to it. What should he test first?
choices: Whether the section would still seem worth keeping if someone else had written it
Whether attachment proves the section has hidden quality
Whether every draft should be preserved out of fairness

explanation.gentle: Right. He needs to judge the section from outside ownership.
explanation.direct: The useful check is whether the passage survives once authorship is removed from the evaluation.
explanation.competitive: Good. Take his name off the paragraph and make it fight clean.

questions.prompt: Nora lists her old sofa for far above nearby sale prices because it still feels valuable to her household. Which principle explains the gap best?
choices: Neutral buyers are irrationally cheap
Ownership is adding emotional exit costs into the valuation
Household goods always deserve sentimental premiums

explanation.gentle: Yes. The asking price is being pushed up by how costly letting go feels.
explanation.direct: That is the key. The valuation is absorbing ownership-based reluctance rather than tracking outside evidence alone.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. The price is billing for exit pain, not just for the sofa.

questions.prompt: What is the cleanest practical correction when a possession feels unusually hard to sell?
choices: Wait until the feeling fades completely before deciding
Ask what you would honestly pay if the item were not already yours
Assume buyers will eventually see the value you see

explanation.gentle: Right. That question helps separate value from ownership feeling.
explanation.direct: A non-owner pricing check is the cleanest way to see whether possession is inflating the number.
explanation.competitive: That is the move. Make the item defend its price without your label on it.

questions.prompt: Which statement stays inside this chapter's boundary?
choices: All attachment to owned things is irrational
Use and replacement cost may matter, but ownership alone should not act like a premium multiplier
Owners can never know anything useful about their possessions

explanation.gentle: Yes. The chapter warns about ownership alone inflating value, not about every real cost or use factor.
explanation.direct: That line preserves the boundary: some support can be real, but possession itself should not quietly do the pricing.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. Utility can count, but the owner bonus does not get to run the number.

questions.prompt: A manager is choosing whether to keep an owned asset that feels expensive to give up. Which earlier chapter's lesson pairs best with the endowment effect here?
choices: Outcome Bias, because a recent good result alone should not decide the asset's value
Liking Bias, because the manager must like the asset personally
Chauffeur Knowledge, because the team may speak confidently about the asset

explanation.gentle: Yes. A recent outcome should not replace a cleaner look at the asset's present value and the ownership distortion around it.
explanation.direct: This pairing works because both chapters warn against letting something adjacent to quality or value stand in for direct evaluation.
explanation.competitive: That is the strongest link. A lucky result and an owner bonus can both fake the score.

questions.prompt: A fair valuation survives which test?
choices: The owner's pride in having chosen or built the item
A promise that the item will always feel special
A non-owner view that still supports the price after possession is mentally removed

explanation.gentle: Yes. The price should still make sense from outside ownership.
explanation.direct: That is the decisive test because it asks whether the valuation can stand once possession stops doing hidden work.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. If the number folds without your label on it, it was never standing clean.
